title: Computer Science: Unit-wise Subjective Question Bank
html:
Group A is ten single marks.

The other 40 marks of the Computer Science paper come from ten short questions of 2 marks (Group B) and five long questions of 4 marks (Group C), and here the marker gives one mark for each correct key element of your answer: a definition, a difference, an example, a correct line of code, a correct output.

This chapter works through the five units in syllabus order. Each section opens with a fully worked model question, then gives 2-mark and 4-mark questions with complete answers.

How to use this bank

Read the model question at the head of each unit, then close the book and write the other answers yourself.

Mark them by key element: a 2-mark difference needs two separate, complete points; a [1+3] question needs the definition plus three explained points.

Every program and query here was run (Python 3.12, MySQL 8.4) and its output is printed: compare yours line by line. A 2-mark question deserves about 4 minutes and a 4-mark question about 8.

Practice items, not past questions

Every question below is an original practice item written to the CDC grid and model paper. None is claimed to have appeared in an SEE paper.

21.1 Computer Network and Communication

Model question: planning a small network

Problem. A health post in a rural municipality has four computers, a printer and a Wi-Fi access point. There is no fibre line, so it will use a 4G router for the Internet.

Plan the network: name the topology, the devices and media, and explain how the computers get their IP addresses. [4]

Solution. (1) Topology: a star, with an 8-port switch at the centre, because one faulty cable then affects only one computer and devices are easy to add.

(2) Media and devices: CAT6 cables with RJ-45 connectors from each computer, the printer and the access point to the switch; the 4G router connects the switch to the mobile network, so it is the default gateway.

(3) Addressing: the router's DHCP server gives each computer a dynamic private address such as 192.168.1.10, while the printer is given a static address (192.168.1.20) so that everyone can always find it.

(4) Wi-Fi: staff phones and laptops join through the access point, protected by a WPA2/WPA3 password. One mark for each numbered point.

Short questions (2 marks each)

  1. Define bandwidth and throughput. [2]
  2. Differentiate between simplex and half-duplex communication with one example each. [2]
  3. Give two reasons for joining two school buildings 500 m apart with optical fibre. [2]
  4. Write two differences between a switch and a router. [2]
  5. A 1.2 GB software update downloads at 50 Mbps. Find the time in minutes (take 1 GB = 1,000 MB). [2]
  6. Differentiate between IPv4 and IPv6 in two points. [2]
  7. What are the uses of the ping and ipconfig commands? [2]
  8. Differentiate between an intranet and an extranet with one example each. [2]

Long questions (4 marks each)

  1. Explain any four network topologies, with a sketch and one advantage of each. [4]
  2. What are guided and unguided media? Give two examples of each and write two differences. [1+1+2]
  3. Define IP address. Explain private and public, and static and dynamic, addresses with examples. [1+3]
  4. Compare client–server and peer-to-peer networks. Which one should a bank use, and why? [3+1]
Solutions to 21.1

Short 1. Bandwidth is the maximum amount of data a link can carry per second; throughput is the amount actually delivered per second. Both are measured in bps, Mbps or Gbps.

Short 2. Simplex: data flows in one direction only, e.g. TV broadcasting. Half duplex: data flows both ways but one way at a time, e.g. a walkie-talkie.

Short 3. Copper Ethernet is limited to 100 m per run, while fibre carries data for kilometres; and fibre carries light, so lightning and electrical noise between the buildings cannot disturb it (it is also faster).

Short 4. A switch joins devices within one LAN and forwards frames by MAC address; a router joins different networks (a LAN and the Internet) and forwards packets by IP address, choosing the best path.

Short 5. 1.2 GB = 1,200 MB = 1,200 × 8 = 9,600 Mb; time = 9,600 ÷ 50 = 192 s = 3.2 minutes.

Short 6. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, written as four decimal numbers with dots (192.168.1.1); IPv6 addresses are 128 bits, written as eight hexadecimal groups with colons (2001:db8::1). IPv4 offers about 4.3 billion addresses, IPv6 about 3.4 × 10³⁸.

Short 7. ping checks whether another computer or website can be reached and shows the time each reply takes; ipconfig shows this computer's IP address, subnet mask and default gateway.

Short 8. An intranet is a private network for an organisation's own staff, e.g. a bank's staff portal; an extranet opens part of it to selected outsiders, e.g. a supplier portal where shops check their orders.

Long 1.

Bus all nodes on one backbone cable with terminators — uses the least cable.

Ring each node joined to the next in a closed loop, data in one direction — no collisions.

Star every node cabled to a central switch — one faulty cable affects only one computer and faults are easy to find.

Mesh nodes joined by many links — data takes another path if a link fails. (A tree or hybrid is also acceptable.) Each needs a small labelled sketch.

Long 2. Guided media carry signals along a cable — twisted pair, coaxial, optical fibre. Unguided media carry electromagnetic waves through air or space — radio, microwave, infrared, satellite, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth.

Differences: guided media give a fixed path and are little affected by weather, while unguided signals spread out and are weakened by walls and rain; guided media are harder to tap, while unguided media allow devices to move freely.

Long 3. An IP address is the logical number given to every device on a network to identify it and route data to it.

Private addresses (10.x, 172.16–31.x, 192.168.x) are used inside LANs and not routed on the Internet; public addresses are unique worldwide and assigned by ISPs, e.g. 8.8.8.8.

Static addresses are set by hand and never change, e.g. a printer at 192.168.1.20; dynamic addresses are given by DHCP for a lease period, e.g. a phone joining Wi-Fi.

Long 4. Client–server: dedicated servers provide services to clients; central control, strong security and central backup; costly; suits large networks.

Peer-to-peer: all computers equal, each shares its own resources; cheap and simple, but weak security and separate backups; suits about ten computers.

A bank must use client–server, because customer accounts need central security, access control, backup and many simultaneous users.

21.2 Database Management System

Model question: SQL for a library table

Problem. A school library keeps library(book_id, title, author, price, copies). Write SQL to(a) create the table with book_id as primary key, title required and price greater than 0;(b) add the book 5, "Shirishko Phool" by Parijat, Rs 300, 3 copies;(c) show the title and price of books costing more than Rs 500, the most expensive first;(d) add two copies of book 2. [4]

Solution.

CREATE TABLE library (
    book_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    title   VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL,
    author  VARCHAR(40),
    price   DECIMAL(7, 2) CHECK (price > 0),
    copies  INT DEFAULT 1
);
INSERT INTO library (book_id, title, author, price, copies)
VALUES (5, 'Shirishko Phool', 'Parijat', 300.00, 3);
SELECT title, price FROM library WHERE price > 500 ORDER BY price DESC;
UPDATE library SET copies = copies + 2 WHERE book_id = 2;

Tested with four more books in the table, the SELECT returned:

title price
Karnali Blues 700.00
Palpasa Cafe 650.00
Seto Dharti 550.00

and the UPDATE reported 1 row affected, raising Palpasa Cafe from 2 to 4 copies. One mark for each correct statement.

Short questions (2 marks each)

  1. Define primary key and foreign key with one example each. [2]
  2. Write two differences between DDL and DML, naming two commands of each. [2]
  3. Write two advantages of a DBMS over a paper filing system. [2]
  4. What is a composite key? When is it needed? Give an example. [2]
  5. Write an SQL statement to display the names of students that begin with S from students(roll, name, class). [2]
  6. What is the difference between DELETE and DROP? [2]
  7. Name the type of relationship, with a reason:(a) a citizen and his or her citizenship certificate;(b) a class teacher and the students of the class. [2]

Long questions (4 marks each)

  1. Define DBMS. Explain any three of its features. [1+3]
  2. A school keeps staff(sid, name, post, salary). Write SQL to(a) show the name and salary of staff earning from Rs 30,000 to Rs 50,000;(b) list all names in alphabetical order;(c) change the post of sid 5 to "Head";(d) remove all staff whose post is "Peon". [4]
  3. Explain the three types of relationship with an example of each, and state how each is stored in tables. [4]
Solutions to 21.2

Short 1. A primary key uniquely identifies each record and cannot be NULL, e.g. roll in students. A foreign key is a field that refers to the primary key of another table, e.g. roll in marks referring to students(roll).

Short 2. DDL defines the structure of the database — CREATE, ALTER, DROP; DML works on the data in the tables — INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE. DDL changes are committed at once; DML changes can be undone inside a transaction.

Short 3. Searching, sorting and updating take seconds instead of hours; and keys and constraints stop duplicate or invalid entries (also security, backup, many users at once).

Short 4. A composite key is a key made of two or more fields that together identify a record; it is needed when no single field is unique, e.g. (roll, subject) in a marks table, where a student has many subjects.

Short 5.

SELECT name FROM students WHERE name LIKE 'S%';

On the students table of the DBMS chapter it returned Subigya Nepal and Sampada Bhattarai.

Short 6. DELETE (DML) removes chosen rows or all rows but keeps the table; DROP (DDL) removes the whole table, its structure and data, permanently.

Short 7. (a) One-to-one — each citizen has one certificate and each certificate belongs to one citizen. (b) One-to-many — one class teacher has many students, but each student has one class teacher.

Long 1. A DBMS is software that creates, stores, retrieves, updates and manages data in a database, e.g. MySQL.

Features: data storage in tables of rows and columns; data retrieval with queries in seconds; data integrity through keys and constraints such as CHECK; security through accounts and permissions; backup and recovery; control of redundancy (any three, one mark each).

Long 2.

SELECT name, salary FROM staff WHERE salary BETWEEN 30000 AND 50000;
SELECT name FROM staff ORDER BY name;
UPDATE staff SET post = 'Head' WHERE sid = 5;
DELETE FROM staff WHERE post = 'Peon';

On six sample records, (a) returned Gita Sharma 42000.00, Hari Thapa 38000.00 and Mohan Rai 46000.00; (b) listed Bina KC, Gita Sharma, Hari Thapa, Mohan Rai, Ram Lama, Sita Magar; (c) changed 1 row; (d) removed 2 rows, leaving four staff.

Long 3.

One-to-one one record matches exactly one, e.g. person — passport; stored by putting one table's primary key as a unique foreign key in the other.

One-to-many one record matches many, each of which matches one, e.g. teacher — classes; the foreign key goes in the "many" table.

Many-to-many many match many, e.g. students — courses; stored with a junction table enrolment(roll, course_code) holding both keys.

21.3 Multimedia

Model question: which audio format to send?

Problem. A 3-minute song is recorded in stereo at 44.1 kHz and 16 bits.(a) Find its size as a WAV file.(b) Find its size as a 128 kbps MP3.(c) Which should be sent on WhatsApp, and which kept for editing? [2+1+1]

Solution.(a) Size = 44,100 × 16 × 2 × 180 = 254,016,000 bits; ÷ 8 = 31,752,000 bytes ≈ 31.8 MB.(b) 128,000 × 180 = 23,040,000 bits; ÷ 8 = 2,880,000 bytes ≈ 2.9 MB, about 11 times smaller.(c) Send the MP3: small and plays everywhere. Keep the WAV for editing, because it is uncompressed and every edit and re-save of an MP3 loses more quality.

Short questions (2 marks each)

  1. Define multimedia. Write two of its uses in business. [2]
  2. Write two differences between raster and vector graphics. [2]
  3. What is the difference between lossy and lossless compression? Name one format of each. [2]
  4. What are the frame rate and the resolution of a video? [2]
  5. Why is PNG preferred for a logo on a website, while JPG is preferred for a photograph? [2]
  6. What is typography? Write two typography rules for a poster. [2]
  7. Write two differences between 2D and 3D animation. [2]

Long questions (4 marks each)

  1. Explain the steps to make a poster in Pixlr: creating the project, adding text and a shape, using layers, and exporting it. [4]
  2. A 3-minute Full HD video is recorded at 30 fps. Find(a) the number of frames,(b) the uncompressed size of one frame at 24-bit colour, and(c) the file size at 10 Mbps;(d) explain why video is compressed. [4]
  3. Differentiate between frame-by-frame and keyframe animation with an example. Write two uses of animation in education. [2+2]
Solutions to 21.3

Short 1. Multimedia is the combined use of text, graphics, audio, video and animation to present information. In business it is used for advertisements and product videos, and for presentations and video meetings.

Short 2. Raster graphics are grids of pixels and pixelate when enlarged; vector graphics are mathematical shapes and stay sharp at any size. Raster suits photographs (JPG, PNG), vector suits logos (SVG).

Short 3. Lossless compression makes a file smaller without losing any detail (PNG, FLAC); lossy compression throws away detail that is hard to notice, giving much smaller files (JPG, MP3).

Short 4. Frame rate is the number of frames shown each second (fps), e.g. 30 fps; resolution is the number of pixels in each frame, width × height, e.g. 1920 × 1080.

Short 5. PNG is lossless and supports a transparent background, so a logo keeps sharp edges and sits cleanly on any colour. JPG's lossy compression makes photographs much smaller with no visible loss, while PNG photos would be very large.

Short 6. Typography is the art of arranging text for readability and appearance. Rules: use at most two fonts; make headings much larger than body text, with strong contrast between text and background.

Short 7. 2D animation has width and height only and looks flat; 3D has depth, perspective, light and shadow. 2D is drawn or built from flat parts; 3D is modelled, rigged and rendered.

Long 1. (1) Open pixlr.com → Pixlr Express → Create new; type a name and a size such as 1920 × 1080 → Create.

(2) Choose the Text tool → Add new text, type the title and set font, size and colour; add a shape from Arrange/Elements → Shape and set its fill.

(3) In the Layers panel add, rename, hide, lock or reorder layers so that the background, photo and text stay separate. (4) Click Save, choose PNG (or JPG), set the quality and Save as.

Long 2. (a) 3 × 60 × 30 = 5,400 frames. (b) 1920 × 1080 × 3 = 6,220,800 bytes (about 6.2 MB). (c) 10,000,000 × 180 = 1,800,000,000 bits; ÷ 8 = 225,000,000 bytes = 225 MB.

(d) Uncompressed, the video would need 6.2 MB × 5,400 ≈ 33.6 GB; codecs such as H.264 make it small enough to store, upload and stream.

Long 3. Frame-by-frame animation draws every frame separately, e.g. a hand-drawn cartoon at 24 drawings per second.

Keyframe animation sets only the key positions and the software calculates the in-between frames, e.g. a ball placed at the start and end of its path.

Uses in education: animated science processes such as the water cycle or a beating heart; simulations and interactive lessons such as E-Paath.

21.4 Programming in Python

Model question: read a pandas program, then change it

Problem. Study the program and answer.

import pandas as pd
data = {"Item": ["Pen", "Copy", "Bag", "Pencil"], "Price": [20, 60, 1200, 10]}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)
print(df[df["Price"] < 50])

(a) Write its output.(b) Modify it to show the items costing Rs 50 or more, the most expensive first. [2+2]

Solution. (a)

     Item  Price
0     Pen     20
3  Pencil     10

Only rows whose Price is below 50 are kept, with their original index numbers.

(b)

import pandas as pd
data = {"Item": ["Pen", "Copy", "Bag", "Pencil"], "Price": [20, 60, 1200, 10]}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)
costly = df[df["Price"] >= 50]
print(costly.sort_values("Price", ascending=False))

   Item  Price
2   Bag   1200
1  Copy     60

Short questions (2 marks each)

  1. Write a function simple_interest(p, t, r) that returns the simple interest, and call it for p = 5000, t = 2, r = 10. [2]
  2. Write a program that reads the user's age and uses try-except to handle a ValueError when letters are typed. [2]
  3. Write the output of the following program, showing how you got it. [2]
total = 1
for i in range(1, 5):
    total *= i
print(total)
  1. Differentiate between a local and a global variable with an example. [2]
  2. What is the difference between the file modes "w" and "a"? [2]
  3. Write a turtle program to draw a square of side 120 using a loop. [2]
  4. Write a program that reads marks.csv (columns Name, Marks) with pandas and prints the average mark. [2]
  5. Why is a bar chart suitable for comparing the population of Nepal's seven provinces? [2]

Long questions (4 marks each)

  1. Write a program with a function grade(p) that returns the SEE letter grade for a percentage p, and use it to print the grades of 55, 82.5, 91 and 33. [4]
  2. Write a pandas program that makes a DataFrame of four students' Name, Club and Score, saves it as club.csv without the index, reads it back and shows the students who scored more than 70. [4]
  3. A family spends Rs 15,000 on food, 10,000 on rent, 8,000 on education and 7,000 on other things each month. Write a program to draw a pie chart with a title and percentages, and state the percentage for food. [3+1]
  4. Write a program that asks for a file name, displays the file, shows a message if the file does not exist, and always prints "Done" at the end. [4]
Solutions to 21.4

Short 1.

def simple_interest(p, t, r):
    return p * t * r / 100

print("Simple interest:", simple_interest(5000, 2, 10))

Output: Simple interest: 1000.0.

Short 2.

try:
    age = int(input("Enter your age: "))
    print("In five years you will be", age + 5)
except ValueError:
    print("Please type your age in digits, for example 15.")

Typing "fifteen" prints the message; typing 15 prints In five years you will be 20.

Short 3. The loop multiplies total by 1, 2, 3 and 4: 1 × 1 × 2 × 3 × 4 = 24 (it computes 4!).

Short 4. A local variable is created inside a function and exists only there; a global variable is created outside all functions and can be read anywhere. In x = 10 followed by def f(): y = 5, x is global and y is local — print(y) outside f gives a NameError.

Short 5. "w" erases the file's old content and writes from the start; "a" keeps the old content and adds the new data at the end. Both create the file if it does not exist.

Short 6.

import turtle
t = turtle.Turtle()
for i in range(4):
    t.forward(120)
    t.right(90)
turtle.done()

Short 7.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("marks.csv")
print("Average marks:", df["Marks"].mean())

With marks 78, 64, 91 and 55 it printed Average marks: 72.0.

Short 8. The provinces are separate categories to be compared, and bars of different lengths show at a glance which province has the most and the fewest people; a line chart would wrongly suggest a trend between provinces.

Long 1.

def grade(p):
    if p >= 90:
        return "A+"
    elif p >= 80:
        return "A"
    elif p >= 70:
        return "B+"
    elif p >= 60:
        return "B"
    elif p >= 50:
        return "C+"
    elif p >= 40:
        return "C"
    elif p >= 35:
        return "D"
    else:
        return "NG"

for p in [55, 82.5, 91, 33]:
    print(p, "->", grade(p))

55 -> C+
82.5 -> A
91 -> A+
33 -> NG

Long 2.

import pandas as pd

data = {"Name": ["Asmita", "Bijay", "Chandani", "Dipesh"],
        "Club": ["Science", "Sports", "Coding", "Eco"],
        "Score": [78, 64, 91, 70]}
pd.DataFrame(data).to_csv("club.csv", index=False)

df = pd.read_csv("club.csv")
print(df[df["Score"] > 70])

       Name     Club  Score
0    Asmita  Science     78
2  Chandani   Coding     91

Dipesh's 70 is not more than 70, so he is left out.

Long 3.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

items = ["Food", "Rent", "Education", "Others"]
amount = [15000, 10000, 8000, 7000]

plt.pie(amount, labels=items, autopct="%1.1f%%")
plt.title("Monthly expenses of a family")
plt.show()

Food is 15,000 ÷ 40,000 × 100 = 37.5 %, the largest slice.

Long 4.

name = input("Enter file name: ")
try:
    f = open(name, "r")
    print(f.read())
    f.close()
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("File", name, "was not found.")
finally:
    print("Done")

For a missing file it printed File notes.txt was not found. and then Done; for an existing file it printed the file's contents and then Done.

21.5 AI and Contemporary Technologies

Model question: AI cameras for traffic

Problem. A municipality wants to use AI cameras to manage traffic and to detect vehicles breaking the rules. Write two benefits and two ethical concerns, with a safeguard for each concern. [2+2]

Solution.

Benefits (1) traffic lights can adjust to the real flow of vehicles, reducing jams and fuel waste; (2) rule-breakers are detected day and night, making roads safer.

Concerns and safeguards (1) privacy — cameras record everyone's movements; keep only the footage needed, delete it after a fixed period and allow only authorised officers to view it; (2) bias and errors — the system may misread number plates or faces in poor light or for some groups; have a human officer check every fine before it is issued and test the system's accuracy regularly.

Short questions (2 marks each)

  1. Define artificial intelligence and machine learning. [2]
  2. Differentiate between supervised and unsupervised learning, with an example of each. [2]
  3. What is reinforcement learning? Give an example. [2]
  4. Write two limitations of generative AI. [2]
  5. Write the three stages of the sense–think–act cycle of a robot. [2]
  6. What is the Internet of Things? Give two examples of IoT in a home. [2]
  7. Differentiate between virtual reality and augmented reality. [2]
  8. Differentiate between IaaS and SaaS with an example of each. [2]
  9. Write two merits of e-governance with examples from Nepal. [2]

Long questions (4 marks each)

  1. Explain how a large language model and an image generator produce their output. Write two tips for writing a good prompt. [2+2]
  2. Explain the three cloud service models with an example of each. Which would a school use to prepare its routine, and why? [3+1]
  3. Discuss the use of IoT in smart agriculture in Nepal with two examples, and write two challenges of IoT. [2+2]
Solutions to 21.5

Short 1. AI is the branch of computer science that makes machines do tasks needing human intelligence, such as reasoning and understanding language. ML is the part of AI in which machines learn from data and improve with experience.

Short 2. Supervised learning trains on labelled data, e.g. emails marked spam or not spam; unsupervised learning finds groups in unlabelled data, e.g. grouping customers by shopping habits.

Short 3. Reinforcement learning is learning by trial and error: an agent acts, receives rewards or penalties, and learns the actions that earn most reward — e.g. a robot learning to walk or a program learning to play a game.

Short 4. It can produce false information confidently (hallucination); and it can repeat bias from its training data (also out-of-date knowledge, privacy risks, copyright issues).

Short 5. Sense: sensors collect information; think: the controller or AI decides what to do; act: actuators such as motors carry out the action.

Short 6. IoT is the network of everyday objects with sensors and Internet connections that collect and share data and act on it. Home examples: smart bulbs or plugs controlled from a phone; a doorbell camera that sends alerts.

Short 7. VR replaces the real world with a computer-made 3D world seen through a headset, e.g. a VR game; AR adds digital information on top of the real world through a phone or glasses, e.g. Google Lens translating a sign.

Short 8. IaaS provides virtual servers, storage and networks managed by the customer's IT staff, e.g. Amazon EC2; SaaS provides complete applications used through a browser, e.g. Gmail or Google Docs.

Short 9. Faster service without queues, e.g. applying for a passport online; and transparency, e.g. tracking applications and seeing SEE results online (also less corruption, and services such as the Nagarik App from any district).

Long 1. An LLM is trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next token (word piece); when given a prompt it writes the answer one token at a time, choosing likely tokens, so it does not look facts up.

An image generator (diffusion model) learns from pictures and captions; it starts from random noise and removes the noise step by step, guided by the prompt, until an image forms.

Prompt tips: state the task, audience, length and format clearly; give context or an example, and refine the prompt if the first answer is not right.

Long 2.

IaaS virtual servers, storage and networks on rent, managed by your own IT staff — Amazon EC2.

PaaS a ready platform to build and run applications — Google App Engine.

SaaS finished software used online — Gmail, Google Docs. A school would use SaaS such as Google Docs or Sheets to prepare its routine: nothing to install, teachers can edit and view it from anywhere, and it is free or cheap.

Long 3. Soil-moisture sensors in a field can switch irrigation pumps on only when the soil is dry, saving water and electricity for farmers in the Terai; and temperature and humidity sensors in a greenhouse or poultry farm can send alerts to the farmer's phone so that conditions are corrected in time (also livestock trackers, crop-disease alerts).

Challenges: devices need reliable Internet and electricity, which villages may lack; and connected devices can be hacked and the cost is high for small farmers.

21.6 Extended model answers (10 marks)

The Computer Science paper asks for 7 to 8 point explanations, complete Python programs and device descriptions. Each model below has an introduction, explained points with Nepali examples, a table and a conclusion.

Extended questions

  1. What is artificial intelligence? Explain its applications with examples from Nepal, and write its limitations. [10]
  2. Write Python programs to check whether a number is prime, to find a factorial, and to find the total, average and highest of five marks. [10]
  3. What is a transmission medium? Explain the guided and unguided media with examples. [10]

Model answer D1: artificial intelligence (10 marks)

Introduction. Artificial intelligence (AI) is the ability of a computer or a machine to do tasks that normally need human intelligence, such as learning, reasoning, understanding speech and recognising pictures.

It learns from large amounts of data instead of following only fixed instructions. The term was first used by John McCarthy in 1956.

Applications.

  1. Education. AI tutors and apps check answers, explain a mistake and set the next exercise for each student. Teachers in Nepal use online platforms and translation tools to prepare lessons.
  2. Health. AI reads X-rays and scans, and helps doctors find diseases early. Mobile apps give first advice in remote villages where a doctor is far away.
  3. Agriculture. Cameras and sensors tell a farmer about crop disease and the right time to water. This can raise the yield of rice, maize and vegetables in the Terai.
  4. Banking and payment. Banks and wallets such as eSewa and Fonepay use AI to catch strange transactions and warn about fraud.
  5. Transport. Navigation apps predict traffic in Kathmandu and suggest a faster route. Self-driving vehicles are being tested in many countries.
  6. Voice assistants and translation. Assistants understand speech, and apps translate English into Nepali in seconds.
  7. Industry and robotics. Robots weld, paint and pack goods without rest, as the robot arm in the photograph does.
  8. Disaster management. AI studies satellite images and weather data to warn about floods and landslides, which helps the monsoon response in Nepal.

Limitations.

Limitation Explanation
Job loss Machines may replace routine work
Costly Data, hardware and skilled staff are expensive
No feeling or common sense AI cannot truly understand emotions or ethics
Bias It repeats the mistakes of the data it learned from
Privacy Large personal data can be misused
Dependence People may stop thinking for themselves

Conclusion. AI is a powerful helper in education, health and farming. It must be used with care, honesty and human control, and Nepal should prepare its youth with coding and data skills.

Model answer D2: Python programs (10 marks)

Introduction. Python is a high-level, interpreted language with simple syntax, widely used in schools and in AI. Programs use input, decision (if), loops (for) and lists. The programs below were run and the outputs are shown.

Program 1: prime number.

n = 29
if n < 2:
    print(n, "is not prime")
else:
    for i in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1):
        if n % i == 0:
            print(n, "is not prime; divisible by", i)
            break
    else:
        print(n, "is prime")

Output: 29 is prime

A number is prime if no number from 2 up to its square root divides it. The else of the loop runs only when the loop ends without break.

Program 2: factorial of 5.

f = 1

Model answer D3: transmission media (10 marks)

Introduction. A transmission medium is the path through which data travels from the sender to the receiver in a network.

It is of two kinds: guided (wired) media, where the signal follows a cable, and unguided (wireless) media, where the signal moves through air or space.

Guided media.

  1. Twisted-pair cable (UTP). Four pairs of copper wires twisted to reduce noise and ending in an RJ-45 plug. It is cheap and used in school labs up to 100 m.
  2. Coaxial cable. A copper core with insulation and a metal shield. It is used for cable TV and older networks.
  3. Optical fibre. A thin glass thread that carries pulses of light. It is very fast, free from electrical noise and used for the Internet backbone and ISP connections to homes.

Unguided media.

  1. Radio waves. Used for FM radio, Wi-Fi and mobile networks; they pass through walls.
  2. Microwaves. Used for towers of Nepal Telecom and Ncell in a line of sight.
  3. Infrared. Short range, used in a TV remote.
  4. Satellite. Used for DishHome and for communication in remote mountain areas.

Comparison

Basis Twisted pair Coaxial Optical fibre Wireless
Speed Medium Medium-high Very high Medium
Cost Low Medium High Medium
Range 100 m 500 m Many km Depends
Noise Affected Less affected Not affected Affected
Security Medium Medium High Low unless encrypted

Conclusion. Twisted pair suits a lab, fibre suits long distance and high speed, and wireless gives mobility. A good network often mixes all of them.
